Consider the question: which policy type should you change first when traffic follows an unexpected path?

Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › SD-WAN Policy Configuration
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

SD-WAN Policy Configuration

Discover how centralized control policies define topology, how centralized data policies steer traffic at packet time, and why local policies remain essential for device-level needs. Learn practical safety checks and a short hands-on conceptual walkthrough for a simple data policy.

Policy Flow Overview
How control and data policies shape the fabric
vManage → vSmart
Centralized control policies alter OMP routes and TLOC attributes before distribution.
vSmart → vEdge/cEdge
Centralized data policies instruct devices how to handle packets and steer traffic.
Local Device Rules
Device-applied ACLs, NAT, and QoS refine behavior for a specific router.
Explore Key Topics
Centralized Control
Filter and modify OMP routes, control TLOC reachability, enforce hub-and-spoke topologies.
Centralized Data
Application-aware routing, QoS, and service chaining to shape user experience.
Local Policies
ACLs, NAT, and interface QoS for device-specific needs and last-mile controls.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives guide practical skill building. First, you will be able to differentiate the three policy families: centralized control, centralized data, and local policies. That distinction matters because each family operates in a different plane and affects routes, packets, or device behavior respectively. Second, you will understand how centralized control policies influence OMP route advertisements and TLOC selection. You will learn concrete examples such as filtering prefixes and preventing branch-to-branch TLOC reachability to shape a hub-and-spoke topology. Third, you will explain how centralized data policies implement application-aware routing, QoS, and service chaining so that critical apps get the right path and security services. We'll show how an AAR profile can fail traffic over to a backup transport when thresholds are breached. Fourth, you will describe local policies for device-specific traffic manipulation including ACLs, NAT, and QoS on interfaces. Knowing when to use local policies prevents global misconfiguration and secures local services. Each objective will include a verification milestone so you can confirm competency.

Competency Checks

Short lab-style verifications you can run conceptually to confirm each objective.

01 Scenario: Prevent Spoke-to-Spoke
Design a control policy that restricts TLOC advertisements from branches to other branches and validate by checking OMP reachability tables.
Checkpoint: Confirm branches only see data center prefixes.
02 Control Policy Filter
Build a route filter and explain the effect on path selection and FIB population at remote sites.
Checkpoint: Verify no unintended route withdrawal.
03 Data Policy AAR Test
Author a rule that prefers MPLS for a critical app and fails over to internet when SLA thresholds are crossed.
Checkpoint: Simulate loss/latency and observe failover.
04 Local Policy Validation
Apply an ACL and NAT on a device and confirm that only intended traffic is permitted and translated.
Checkpoint: Ensure default-action presence to avoid accidental drops.

screens.title: What is a Policy in SD-WAN?
screens.narratorSegment: A policy in SD-WAN is a rule set that controls how routing information is advertised, how data packets are forwarded, or how a device behaves locally. In other words, policies map intent—like prefer MPLS for VoIP or force branch traffic through a firewall—into concrete configuration actions. Policies differ by scope and plane. Control policies alter the control plane: they change OMP attributes, filter prefixes, or control which TLOCs can form tunnels, thereby shaping the logical topology. Data policies operate on the data plane and inspect packet attributes such as application, ports, or DSCP to decide forwarding, marking, or chaining through services. Local policies are device-specific and implement access control lists, NAT, or interface QoS. A concrete example: to prevent branches from forming spokes to each other, you use a control policy to stop branch TLOC routes from being advertised to other branches. A common misconception is to treat all policies as equivalent; that leads to placing a packet steering rule in a control policy where it will have no effect. The core takeaway: choose the right policy family for your goal—routing, packet steering, or local device behavior—and always include a default action to avoid accidental drops.

content.html:
Core Concept What is a Policy in SD-WAN?

Policy definition and role

Policies are the mechanism to enforce routing, forwarding, and device-level rules across the SD-WAN fabric.

Three policy families
  • Centralized control policies: Change OMP attributes, filter routes, and control topology before distribution.
  • Centralized data policies: Inspect and act on packets for AAR, QoS, and service chaining on devices.
  • Local policies: Device-specific ACLs, NAT, and interface QoS applied directly on vEdge or cEdge.
Concrete example
Preventing direct branch-to-branch tunnels is a routing intent implemented with a centralized control policy that limits TLOC visibility.
Explanation bullets
Control policies are evaluated before data plane decisions and shape which routes devices even learn.
Data policies run on received packets and can steer traffic dynamically using SLA checks and application matching.
Local policies apply last in the device processing chain for ingress or egress adjustments specific to one router.
Key Takeaway

Pick the policy family that matches your intent: control for route visibility, data for packet steering, and local for device-only adjustments.

screens.title: Centralized Control Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Centralized control policies are authored in vManage and applied by vSmart to the control plane. Their domain is OMP routes and TLOC reachability, which means they decide which routes are advertised to which sites and how route attributes like preference or metric are presented. Think of them as the network's route police: they can filter prefixes, increase or decrease preference to steer best-path selection, or block TLOCs to prevent direct tunnels between sites. A concrete example: to enforce a hub-and-spoke topology, create a control policy that prevents branch TLOCs from being advertised to other branches while allowing the data center TLOCs to be visible everywhere. A common misconception is to expect a control policy to immediately change packet forwarding on a device; rather, it changes what routes the device learns, and that change then affects the forwarding table. Always test control policies by previewing OMP route advertisements and confirming that FIB entries update as expected. When designing control policies, document which site lists and VPN lists are targeted and watch for unintended route withdrawals. The takeaway: control policies shape topology by controlling route visibility and attributes, not by inspecting packets.

keyIdea.title: Control policies shape topology
keyIdea.text: They flip which routes are visible and adjust attributes that determine best-path selection across the fabric.

content.html:
Definition Centralized Control Policies

Control policies affect route advertisements and TLOCs

How they work
  1. Authored in vManage and pushed to vSmart controllers.
  2. Operate on OMP routes and TLOC route advertisements before devices receive them.
  3. Modify attributes (preference, metric) or filter routes to enforce topology.
Concrete example
Prevent branch-to-branch tunnels by filtering branch TLOC advertisements so only data center TLOCs are visible to branches.
Explanation cards
Filter OMP routes: stop specific prefixes from being distributed to a site list.
Modify attributes: change preference or metrics to influence path selection.
Control TLOC reachability: allow or deny which TLOCs form tunnels to enforce topology.
Common mistake
Expecting immediate packet steering from control policies; they only change learned routes and indirectly affect forwarding.

screens.title: Centralized Data Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Centralized data policies operate at packet time on vEdge and cEdge routers. Configured in vManage and distributed by vSmart, these policies inspect packets and apply actions like forwarding to a preferred transport, marking QoS values, or chaining traffic through a service. Application-Aware Routing is a key capability: the data policy can apply an SLA profile that measures loss, latency, and jitter, and then dynamically steer traffic. For instance, voice traffic can prefer MPLS while failing over to internet if latency crosses a threshold. Data policies also implement QoS by marking, policing, or shaping traffic so critical apps receive priority. Service chaining directs traffic to firewalls, IPS, or cloud security gateways in a specified order. Another example is explicit traffic engineering: a data policy can pin a type of traffic to a specific TLOC color for bandwidth or compliance reasons. A misconception is to confuse data policies with control policies; data policies act on packets and require correct direction (from-service or from-tunnel) and correct vpn/site scope. Remember to include default actions in sequences to avoid dropping unmatched traffic. The core takeaway: data policies control the user experience by steering packets where they must go and applying service treatments in-line.

keyIdea.text: They inspect packets, apply SLAs and QoS, and direct traffic through required services to meet application needs.

content.html:
Core Concept Centralized Data Policies

Packet-level steering and service chaining

Key capabilities
  • Application-Aware Routing: Apply SLA profiles and dynamically select transports.
  • QoS: Mark and shape traffic by app, VPN, or DSCP.
  • Service chaining: Direct packets through firewalls or cloud services.
Concrete scenario
If VoIP latency on the business internet exceeds 100ms, a data policy can switch calls to MPLS automatically using an AAR SLA.
Explanation cards
Direction matters: apply data policies 'from-service' to catch LAN-originated flows and 'from-tunnel' for WAN-originated flows.
Default actions: always provide an explicit default accept or drop to avoid accidental traffic loss.
Common mistake: placing AAR logic in a control policy where SLA checks cannot inspect packets.
Key Takeaway

Use centralized data policies to meet application SLAs and to steer traffic dynamically based on measured link quality.

screens.title: Create a Simple Centralized Data Policy (Conceptual Walkthrough)
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a conceptual creation of a centralized data policy that enforces two sequences: HTTP goes over business internet and HTTPS uses MPLS. Start by defining lists: a site list to target branch sites, a VPN list for VPN 10, port lists for HTTP and HTTPS, and TLOC lists or colors for biz-internet and mpls. Next, author sequence 10 to match TCP destination port 80 and VPN 10, then action accept and set tloc-action preferred-color biz-internet. Sequence 20 matches port 443 and sets preferred-color mpls. Always add a default sequence that accepts or explicitly drops other traffic depending on intent. After authoring, assign the policy in the topology to your branch site list and preview the rule. A practical misconception to avoid is forgetting the direction: choose 'from-service' when steering LAN-originated traffic. Another error is omitting a default action, which can drop all unmatched packets. Review the conceptual CLI snippet to confirm structure and then preview on vManage. The takeaway: break the policy into lists, ordered sequences, and a final default action, then validate carefully before activation. Create a Simple Centralized Data Policy (Conceptual Walkthrough) means lists + ordered sequences + actions + default = predictable data policy. always preview before activation.. In practical terms, a conceptual step-by-step example: http prefers biz-internet; https prefers mpls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow Create Data Policy Walkthrough

Conceptual steps and CLI structure

Step-by-step cards
1. Create site-list and vpn-list to target branches and VPN 10.
2. Define application/port lists for HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443).
3. Build ordered sequences: sequence 10 for HTTP -> prefer biz-internet; sequence 20 for HTTPS -> prefer mpls.
4. Add default sequence to accept or explicitly drop unmatched traffic and apply policy 'from-service' to target LAN-originating flows.
Conceptual CLI snippet
policy
 data-policy PREFER_HTTP_HTTPS
  vpn-list vpn10_list
   sequence 10
    match
     destination-port 80
     protocol 6
    !
    action accept
     set
      tloc-action preferred-color biz-internet
     !
   !
   sequence 20
    match
     destination-port 443
     protocol 6
    !
    action accept
     set
      tloc-action preferred-color mpls
     !
   !
   default-action accept
  !
 !
 apply-policy
  site-list branches_site_list
   data-policy PREFER_HTTP_HTTPS from-service
This snippet is a conceptual structure to help you visualize ordered sequences and the final apply-policy block.

screens.title: Local Policies and Uses
screens.narratorSegment: Local policies are the set of rules applied directly on a vEdge or cEdge device, and they are used when a global centralized policy cannot express a device-specific need. Typical uses include access control lists to filter traffic at ingress, NAT for internet access or inter-VPN translation, granular QoS on an interface for a particular uplink, and local route-maps or prefix-lists for routes learned from local LAN protocols. For example, if a branch uses a vendor firewall on-prem that requires specific NAT behavior, implement that NAT as a local policy so it does not affect other sites. Local policies are applied after centralized policies in the processing order, meaning they can act as a final safety net or the first filter on ingress depending on direction. A common pitfall is applying global rules when a local exception is required, causing unnecessary complexity or rule collisions. Always document how local policies interact with centralized ones and test the sequence — because local rules can either refine or override behavior, depending on the exact policy direction and implementation. The takeaway: use local policies for device-specific needs and keep them minimal and well-documented to avoid conflicts.

keyIdea.title: Local = device-specific
keyIdea.text: Use local policies for NIC/interface-level QoS, NAT, ACLs, and local routing overrides that should not be global.

content.html:
Core Concept Local Policies and Uses

When and why to use local policies

Common local policy types
  • ACLs: Filter traffic at the device level to protect local segments.
  • NAT: Implement translations for internet or inter-VPN access specific to the branch.
  • QoS: Apply shaping or queueing per interface for a single router's uplink.
  • Routing adjustments: Local route-maps or prefix-lists for LAN-sourced routes.
Example
A branch firewall requires NAT for internet-bound users. Implement NAT locally so only that site translates addresses, leaving others untouched.
Explanation and pitfalls
Applied after centralized policies in many processing paths; acts as a final touch or first ingress filter depending on direction.
Common mistake: large, undocumented local rule sets that collide with centralized policies and cause unexpected drops.
Pro-tip: keep local policies minimal and use device templates for repeatable, auditable application.
Key Takeaway

Use local policies for unique device-level needs. Keep them small, documented, and tested against centralized rules.

screens.title: Policy Application Order
screens.narratorSegment: Policy order determines which rule wins when multiple policies could affect the same packet or route. A simplified, practical order to remember is: local ingress policies first, then centralized data ingress, centralized control policies that determine routing information, centralized data egress, and local egress policies last. Concretely, when a packet arrives from the LAN, a local from-service policy can filter or mark it, then centralized data policies evaluate application and SLA-based steering. Control policies, while conceptually earlier because they shape route learning, function in the control plane to change what routes devices use. Misunderstanding order often causes admin confusion: for instance, a centralized control policy that hides a route will prevent a data policy from steering traffic to that destination because the device never learned the route. A practical design tip is to map intent to the processing stage you need: change reachability at the control stage, steer packets at the data stage, and apply device fixes at the local stage. Always include default actions and test policy interactions in a lab. The question to keep in mind: which policy should be changed to effect the observed behavior — the packet path, the learned route, or the device rule?

keyIdea.title: Order determines effect
keyIdea.text: Policy type and direction decide when a rule runs. Choose the processing stage that matches your intent to avoid surprises.

content.html:
Process Flow Policy Application Order

A simplified sequence to reason about interactions

Simplified order
  1. Local Policies (Ingress) — first filter or mark packets entering the device.
  2. Centralized Data Policies (Ingress) — apply AAR, QoS, and service chaining to decide forwarding.
  3. Centralized Control Policies — affect what routes the device learns and thus the forwarding table.
  4. Centralized Data Policies (Egress) — optional egress treatments before leaving towards services.
  5. Local Policies (Egress) — final device-specific shaping or ACLs.
Explanation and examples
Example: If a centralized control policy withdraws a route, no data policy can steer packets to that prefix because it's unknown.
Example: An ingress local ACL can block traffic before centralized data policies ever inspect it, which may be intentional for security.
Mistake to avoid: overlapping rules with different directions and scopes that mask the real cause of unexpected behavior.
Key Takeaway

Map each intention to the processing phase where it will be effective, and test interactions in a controlled environment.

screens.title: Control vs Data vs Local: Clear contrasts
screens.narratorSegment: To avoid confusion, contrast the three policy families by scope, operation plane, and typical use case. Centralized control policies operate in the control plane and change OMP advertisements, so they are used when you must change reachability or topology—examples include enforcing hub-and-spoke or restricting which TLOCs can connect. Centralized data policies run on the data plane and examine packets; use them for application-aware routing, QoS assignment, and service chaining to meet performance and security goals. Local policies are device-scoped and applied on the router itself for ACLs, NAT, or interface QoS; they are for exceptions or integration with local appliances. A concrete example: to steer voice traffic dynamically based on loss and latency, choose a centralized data policy with an AAR SLA. Choose the correct policy family by intended effect

Centralized Control
Plane: Control. Scope: Global route visibility. Use: filter prefixes, set preference, enforce topology.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Policy configuration is powerful and potentially risky. The most frequent mistakes are conflicting policies, applying policies to the wrong VPN or site list, omitting default actions, and failing to consider direction. A missing default accept or drop can cause all unmatched traffic to be dropped silently. Another common error is placing packet-steering intent in a control policy so no effect occurs. To stay safe: always preview your policy to see affected routes and forwarding; use small, staged rollouts; keep a rollback plan; and test in a lab. Use clear naming conventions for lists and sequences so it's obvious what each rule targets. For example, when applying an AAR-based data policy, preview which flows match and simulate SLA degradation to verify failover. For control policies, preview OMP advertisements to ensure you do not withdraw critical prefixes inadvertently. Finally, document assumptions and expected outcomes so colleagues can audit changes. The key takeaway: design policies defensively, test before you push, and use small increments with clear rollback steps to avoid enterprise-wide outages. Best Practice Common Mistakes and Safety

Avoiding the big pitfalls

Top mistakes
  • Conflicting or overlapping rules across policy families.
  • Applying a policy to the wrong VPN, site list, or device group.
  • Missing default actions causing silent drops.
  • Confusing control and data policy responsibilities.
Safety checklist
Preview policy effects on OMP and packet matches.
Stage deployments in small site groups and validate behavior.
Keep rollback steps ready and document expected outcomes.

Treat policy changes like software changes: review, test, stage, and roll back when necessary.

fullNarratorScript:
Policies are the central intelligence of Cisco SD-WAN. In this lesson you will learn what each policy type does, why they are applied in a specific order, and how mistakes in policy design can cause widespread outages. First, understand the three policy families: centralized control policies manipulate routing information before it reaches devices; centralized data policies inspect and steer actual packets on devices; and local policies make device-specific adjustments like ACLs, NAT, and interface QoS. You will see a conceptual map showing how vManage pushes configs, how vSmart enforces control policies that alter OMP routes and TLOC attributes, and how vEdge or cEdge devices then apply data and local policies to packets. I will also preview three core topics you will master: route advertisement and topology control, application-aware routing and service chaining, and device-level safety and rollback. By the end, you'll know which policy to use for topology enforcement, for application steering, and for device-specific fixes, and you'll understand a key safety principle: always plan policy order and test changes in a lab before wide deployment. Consider the question: which policy type should you change first when traffic follows an unexpected path?

These learning objectives guide practical skill building. First, you will be able to differentiate the three policy families: centralized control, centralized data, and local policies. That distinction matters because each family operates in a different plane and affects routes, packets, or device behavior respectively. Second, you will understand how centralized control policies influence OMP route advertisements and TLOC selection. You will learn concrete examples such as filtering prefixes and preventing branch-to-branch TLOC reachability to shape a hub-and-spoke topology. Third, you will explain how centralized data policies implement application-aware routing, QoS, and service chaining so that critical apps get the right path and security services. We'll show how an AAR profile can fail traffic over to a backup transport when thresholds are breached. Fourth, you will describe local policies for device-specific traffic manipulation including ACLs, NAT, and QoS on interfaces. Knowing when to use local policies prevents global misconfiguration and secures local services. Each objective will include a verification milestone so you can confirm competency.

This second objectives page frames verification tasks and common pitfalls you will practice. For the policy type differentiation objective, you will explain a real scenario: which policy to change when preventing spoke-to-spoke tunnels — the correct answer is a centralized control policy that modifies TLOC reachability. For control-policy competency, you will design a filter that prevents a prefix from being advertised to select sites and explain the impact on reachability. For data-policy competency, you will author a simple AAR rule or data-policy sequence that prefers a transport color and provides a backup. For local-policy competency, you will craft a device ACL and a NAT entry and describe its effect on traffic flow. Each competency check includes a short lab-style validation: preview policy, simulate a traffic flow, and confirm the observed route and forwarding behavior. Remember to look for common mistakes: missing default actions, wrong direction, or overlapping rules that create unintended drops.

A policy in SD-WAN is a rule set that controls how routing information is advertised, how data packets are forwarded, or how a device behaves locally. In other words, policies map intent—like prefer MPLS for VoIP or force branch traffic through a firewall—into concrete configuration actions. Policies differ by scope and plane. Control policies alter the control plane: they change OMP attributes, filter prefixes, or control which TLOCs can form tunnels, thereby shaping the logical topology. Data policies operate on the data plane and inspect packet attributes such as application, ports, or DSCP to decide forwarding, marking, or chaining through services. Local policies are device-specific and implement access control lists, NAT, or interface QoS. A concrete example: to prevent branches from forming spokes to each other, you use a control policy to stop branch TLOC routes from being advertised to other branches. A common misconception is to treat all policies as equivalent; that leads to placing a packet steering rule in a control policy where it will have no effect. The core takeaway: choose the right policy family for your goal—routing, packet steering, or local device behavior—and always include a default action to avoid accidental drops.

Centralized control policies are authored in vManage and applied by vSmart to the control plane. Their domain is OMP routes and TLOC reachability, which means they decide which routes are advertised to which sites and how route attributes like preference or metric are presented. Think of them as the network's route police: they can filter prefixes, increase or decrease preference to steer best-path selection, or block TLOCs to prevent direct tunnels between sites. A concrete example: to enforce a hub-and-spoke topology, create a control policy that prevents branch TLOCs from being advertised to other branches while allowing the data center TLOCs to be visible everywhere. A common misconception is to expect a control policy to immediately change packet forwarding on a device; rather, it changes what routes the device learns, and that change then affects the forwarding table. Always test control policies by previewing OMP route advertisements and confirming that FIB entries update as expected. When designing control policies, document which site lists and VPN lists are targeted and watch for unintended route withdrawals. The takeaway: control policies shape topology by controlling route visibility and attributes, not by inspecting packets.

Centralized data policies operate at packet time on vEdge and cEdge routers. Configured in vManage and distributed by vSmart, these policies inspect packets and apply actions like forwarding to a preferred transport, marking QoS values, or chaining traffic through a service. Application-Aware Routing is a key capability: the data policy can apply an SLA profile that measures loss, latency, and jitter, and then dynamically steer traffic. For instance, voice traffic can prefer MPLS while failing over to internet if latency crosses a threshold. Data policies also implement QoS by marking, policing, or shaping traffic so critical apps receive priority. Service chaining directs traffic to firewalls, IPS, or cloud security gateways in a specified order. Another example is explicit traffic engineering: a data policy can pin a type of traffic to a specific TLOC color for bandwidth or compliance reasons. A misconception is to confuse data policies with control policies; data policies act on packets and require correct direction (from-service or from-tunnel) and correct vpn/site scope. Remember to include default actions in sequences to avoid dropping unmatched traffic. The core takeaway: data policies control the user experience by steering packets where they must go and applying service treatments in-line.

We'll walk through a conceptual creation of a centralized data policy that enforces two sequences: HTTP goes over business internet and HTTPS uses MPLS. Start by defining lists: a site list to target branch sites, a VPN list for VPN 10, port lists for HTTP and HTTPS, and TLOC lists or colors for biz-internet and mpls. Next, author sequence 10 to match TCP destination port 80 and VPN 10, then action accept and set tloc-action preferred-color biz-internet. Sequence 20 matches port 443 and sets preferred-color mpls. Always add a default sequence that accepts or explicitly drops other traffic depending on intent. After authoring, assign the policy in the topology to your branch site list and preview the rule. A practical misconception to avoid is forgetting the direction: choose 'from-service' when steering LAN-originated traffic. Another error is omitting a default action, which can drop all unmatched packets. Review the conceptual CLI snippet to confirm structure and then preview on vManage. The takeaway: break the policy into lists, ordered sequences, and a final default action, then validate carefully before activation. Create a Simple Centralized Data Policy (Conceptual Walkthrough) means lists + ordered sequences + actions + default = predictable data policy. always preview before activation.. In practical terms, a conceptual step-by-step example: http prefers biz-internet; https prefers mpls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Local policies are the set of rules applied directly on a vEdge or cEdge device, and they are used when a global centralized policy cannot express a device-specific need. Typical uses include access control lists to filter traffic at ingress, NAT for internet access or inter-VPN translation, granular QoS on an interface for a particular uplink, and local route-maps or prefix-lists for routes learned from local LAN protocols. For example, if a branch uses a vendor firewall on-prem that requires specific NAT behavior, implement that NAT as a local policy so it does not affect other sites. Local policies are applied after centralized policies in the processing order, meaning they can act as a final safety net or the first filter on ingress depending on direction. A common pitfall is applying global rules when a local exception is required, causing unnecessary complexity or rule collisions. Always document how local policies interact with centralized ones and test the sequence — because local rules can either refine or override behavior, depending on the exact policy direction and implementation. The takeaway: use local policies for device-specific needs and keep them minimal and well-documented to avoid conflicts.

Policy order determines which rule wins when multiple policies could affect the same packet or route. A simplified, practical order to remember is: local ingress policies first, then centralized data ingress, centralized control policies that determine routing information, centralized data egress, and local egress policies last. Concretely, when a packet arrives from the LAN, a local from-service policy can filter or mark it, then centralized data policies evaluate application and SLA-based steering. Control policies, while conceptually earlier because they shape route learning, function in the control plane to change what routes devices use. Misunderstanding order often causes admin confusion: for instance, a centralized control policy that hides a route will prevent a data policy from steering traffic to that destination because the device never learned the route. A practical design tip is to map intent to the processing stage you need: change reachability at the control stage, steer packets at the data stage, and apply device fixes at the local stage. Always include default actions and test policy interactions in a lab. The question to keep in mind: which policy should be changed to effect the observed behavior — the packet path, the learned route, or the device rule?
